questions.q: What specific failure does the TruthfulQA benchmark isolate?
options: A model's tendency to refuse to answer difficult questions
A model confidently reproducing widely held human misconceptions that are well-represented in its training text
A model's inability to perform arithmetic
A model's tendency to change its answer when a user pushes back
questions.explain: TruthfulQA's 817 questions were written to bait answers that match common human misconceptions, testing whether a model reproduces those imitative falsehoods rather than giving the factually correct answer.

questions.q: What inverse-scaling result did the original TruthfulQA paper report?
options: Larger models were consistently more truthful than smaller models on the benchmark
Model size had no measurable effect on truthfulness scores
Larger models were, if anything, slightly less truthful, because scaling helped them imitate human text -- including its errors -- more faithfully
Only the smallest models tested could answer any questions correctly
questions.explain: The paper found that larger models tested were not more truthful and in some cases were slightly less truthful, since scaling improved imitation of training text, including the misconceptions embedded in it.

questions.q: A model is well-calibrated according to this lesson's definition if:
options: It always states 100% confidence regardless of the question
Its stated confidence, averaged across many predictions, roughly matches its actual empirical accuracy at that confidence level
It never answers a question it is unsure about
It always gives the factually correct answer
questions.explain: Calibration specifically means stated confidence tracking real accuracy -- for example, among answers given at 90% stated confidence, roughly 90% should actually be correct.

questions.q: What did Lin, Hilton, and Evans's "Teaching Models to Express Their Uncertainty in Words" demonstrate?
options: That calibration can only ever be measured using a model's raw internal logits
That a model can be trained to state natural-language confidence levels that are themselves well-calibrated, without relying on internal logits
That verbalized confidence is always less accurate than logit-based confidence
That calibration is impossible to achieve in any language model
questions.explain: The study showed GPT-3 could learn to produce verbalized confidence levels (like percentages or qualitative phrases) that mapped to well-calibrated probabilities, holding up reasonably well even under distribution shift.

questions.q: How does this lesson distinguish calibration from truthfulness?
options: They are two names for the exact same measurement

Truthfulness is about whether an answer's content matches known facts; calibration is about whether the model's expressed confidence matches its actual accuracy -- a model can be truthful but overconfident, or untruthful but appropriately hedged
Calibration only applies to math problems, while truthfulness only applies to historical questions
Truthfulness is measured only on closed-source models, and calibration only on open-source models
questions.explain: The two properties are measured on different axes: content correctness (truthfulness) versus the match between expressed confidence and actual accuracy (calibration), and a model's behavior can diverge on these independently.
